title: Forced Vibrations and Resonance
short: Driving near the natural frequency makes the amplitude grow.

blocks.html: Push a spring periodically with a force $F_0\cos\omega t$ and you get $mx'' + cx' + kx = F_0\cos\omega t$, a job for undetermined coefficients. The interesting question is how the response depends on the driving frequency $\omega$ compared with the natural frequency $\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}$ from free vibrations.

Undamped, $\omega \ne \omega_0$: $x_p = \dfrac{F_0}{m(\omega_0^{2} - \omega^{2})}\cos\omega t$; the amplitude grows as $\omega \to \omega_0$.
Resonance, $\omega = \omega_0$: $x_p = \dfrac{F_0}{2m\omega_0}\,t\sin\omega_0t$, which grows without bound.
Damped: the steady response has amplitude $\dfrac{F_0}{\sqrt{(k - m\omega^{2})^{2} + (c\omega)^{2}}}$, largest near $\omega_0$ when $c$ is small.

Try $x_p = A\cos\omega t$ in $mx'' + kx = F_0\cos\omega t$: $(k - m\omega^{2})A = F_0$. This works unless $k = m\omega^{2}$, that is, $\omega = \omega_0$, when $\cos\omega t$ already solves the homogeneous equation; then the guess needs a factor $t$, and the amplitude grows linearly. Starting from rest near resonance, $x$ $= \frac{F_0}{m(\omega_0^{2} - \omega^{2})}(\cos\omega t$ $- \cos\omega_0t)$, and the identity $\cos A - \cos B$ $= 2\sin\frac{B - A}{2}\sin\frac{A + B}{2}$ shows a fast oscillation inside a slow envelope: beats.

blocks.title: Resonance
steps: With $x(0) = x'(0) = 0$ the homogeneous constants are 0.

blocks.title: Damped steady amplitude
blocks.q: Find the steady amplitude for $x'' + 4x' + 4x = 10\cos t$.

blocks.html: Locating resonance at $\omega = k$ or $\omega^{2} = k$ when $m \ne 1$. Resonance happens at $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$. Another slip is keeping the guess $A\cos\omega_0t$ at resonance; it gives $0 = F_0\cos\omega_0t$, the sign that a factor $t$ is needed.

blocks.name: springmass
blocks.cap: A lightly damped spring driven by $F_0\cos\omega t$. With $\omega$ close to $\omega_0 = 2$ the swings grow and fade in beats; set $\omega = 2$ and they build up until damping limits them. Move $\omega$ far from 2 and the response stays small.
